1.open: Think of a project you started with big energy and never quite finished. What was it, and what got in the way?
questions: After Joshua dies, the people ask the LORD, "Who will be the first to go up and fight for us" (v. 1). Why might it matter that they asked before they acted? When do you tend to ask God first, and when do you just move?

Judah asks the Simeonites, "Come up with us," and promises to go with them in return (v. 3). What does this teamwork look like, and where have you seen the same kind of partnership help someone you know?
Adoni-bezek says, "As I have done to them, so God has repaid me" (v. 7). This is a harsh scene. How do you react to it, and what do you think the writer wants us to notice?
Acsah boldly says, "Give me a blessing," and asks for springs of water (v. 15). What do you make of her asking? Is there something you have been slow to ask God or someone else for?

Verse 19 says "The LORD was with Judah," yet they "could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains because they had chariots of iron." Christians read this differently: some see a lapse in trust, others a plain report of real limits. How do you read it, and why?

Verses 27 to 33 repeat the same pattern. Tribe after tribe "failed to drive out" the people, and some pressed them into forced labor instead (v. 28). Why might a group settle for good enough after such a strong start?
Where in your own life, family or church have you stopped short of finishing something because it got hard or inconvenient? Be as honest as you can, and it is fine to say you are not sure.
This chapter has no big villain moment, just a slow slide. What small habits help a person or group keep going in the right direction over many years?
1.life: Pick one thing you started and set aside, whether a habit, a prayer, a relationship or a commitment. This week, take one small step toward it and tell someone in the group so they can check in with you.
1.prayer: Thank God that he is with his people even when they fall short. Ask for the humility to be honest about unfinished things, and the stamina to keep going.
1.tip: The violence in verses 6 to 8 and 17 can take over the whole evening. Name it as hard, acknowledge that readers wrestle with it, then steer back to the chapter's main thread: a strong start that slowly fades. Don't push anyone to feel a certain way about it.

2.open: What is a family tradition or story that gets retold every year, and who makes sure it gets passed on?
questions: The angel says, "I brought you up out of Egypt" and "I will never break My covenant with you" (v. 1). Why do you think the messenger begins by reminding them what God has done before naming what they did wrong?
When the people hear the message, they "lifted up their voices and wept" (v. 4). What do you think they were feeling? Have you ever felt sorry in a way that did not last?

Verse 7 says the people served the LORD as long as Joshua and the elders lived, "who had seen all the great works that the LORD had done for Israel." Whose faith has carried yours along, and what would happen if they were not around?

Verse 10 says another generation arose "who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel." How does a faith get lost in one generation? What helps pass it on, in a family or a church?
Baal and the Ashtoreths were gods people turned to for good harvests and security. What do people around us turn to for those same things today, and where do you feel the pull yourself?

The writer says the LORD "was moved to pity by their groaning" and raised up judges (v. 18), even though the people kept returning to the same habits. What does that show you about how God treats people who keep failing?

This chapter describes a cycle: turning away, trouble, rescue, then turning away again (vv. 11-19). Where do you see a pattern like this in your own life, or in the church today? You can answer honestly, even if your own faith feels thin right now.

Verses 20 to 23 say God left the nations in the land to test Israel. This is a hard idea to sit with. What questions does it raise for you, and what do you do with a passage you do not fully understand?
2.life: This week, tell one person, perhaps a child, a younger friend or a newer believer, a real story of something God has done in your life or in the life of someone you know. Keep it short and plain.
2.prayer: Thank God that he is faithful even when we are not. Ask him to help you remember what he has done and to pass that on to those who come after you.
2.tip: Verses 14, 15 and 20 speak of God's anger and of him handing Israel over to enemies, and this can feel harsh. Do not rush to explain it away or defend it. Name that it is hard, point to verse 18 where God acts from pity, and let people say what troubles them.

3.open: Think of a habit or a group you drifted into slowly, without ever deciding to. How did it happen?
questions: Verse 4 says the nations were left "to test the Israelites, to find out whether they would keep the commandments of the LORD." What do you think it means for God to test his people, and how does that sit with you?
Verses 5 and 6 describe a slow slide: living among the neighbors, marrying them, then serving their gods. What small steps do you think led to that? Where do you see a similar slide today?
Verse 7 says "they forgot the LORD their God." What are the ways a person can forget God without ever deciding to walk away?
In verse 9 "the Israelites cried out to the LORD, " and he raised up a deliverer. What does it tell you about God that he answers people who got themselves into this mess?
The pattern in this chapter repeats: turning away, trouble, crying out, rescue, rest. Where have you seen a pattern like that in your own life or in a church or family?

Ehud's rescue is told in vivid and even mocking detail, and he gets close to the king by saying, "I have a word from God for you" (v. 20). Christians differ on whether the text approves of how he did it or simply reports it. How do you read it, and what makes you uneasy?
The Spirit of the LORD came on Othniel (v. 10), but Ehud and Shamgar are ordinary and unlikely rescuers. What does it say about God that he uses a left-handed man and a farmhand with an oxgoad?
If you are honest, do you ever feel stuck in something with no sign of rescue, or unsure anyone is listening? What would crying out look like for you this week?
3.life: Pick one small habit or influence that may be pulling your heart away from God, and take one step this week to change it. Then, whatever your state of mind, say a short honest prayer asking for help, even if it is only one sentence.
3.prayer: Thank God that he hears when his people cry out, even after they have wandered. Ask him to show each of you where you have been drifting, and to raise up help where it is needed.
3.tip: Ehud's story is graphic, and the group may laugh, squirm or ask whether God approves of the killing. Let people react honestly, say plainly that Christians read this differently, and steer back to the repeating cycle and God's answer to the cry for help (v. 9). If someone feels stuck without rescue, do not rush to fix it.

4.open: Think of a time someone you didn't expect stepped up when it counted. Who was it, and what did they do?
questions: Verses 2 and 3 say Israel was under Jabin's power for twenty years and "cried out to the LORD." When have you waited a long time before asking God for help, and why?
Deborah is introduced as "a prophetess" who was "judging Israel at that time" (v. 4). What does it tell you that God chose her to lead, and how did people come to her (v. 5)?

Barak says, "If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go" (v. 8). Some read this as fear and others as wanting a prophet's backing. How do you read it, and when have you wanted someone beside you before taking a step of faith?
Sisera had "nine hundred chariots of iron" (v. 3), and Israel had nothing like that. What are the big, intimidating things in your life or our community that make you feel outmatched?

Deborah says, "Arise, for this is the day that the LORD has delivered Sisera into your hand. Has not the LORD gone before you?" (v. 14). What would it look like to take a step because you trust God has already gone ahead?

Sisera trusted Jael's tent because of the peace between Jabin and Heber's house (v. 17), and she said, "Do not be afraid" (v. 18). Then she killed him. Christians disagree about whether the story praises Jael or just records what happened. What do you make of it?

Verse 23 says, "On that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites." The writer gives God the credit, even with so many people involved. Where have you seen God work through ordinary or surprising people?
If you are honest, what part of this chapter is hardest for you to read or square with what you know of God? You can pass if you would rather just listen.
4.life: Think of one person who is facing something that feels too big for them. This week, go with them in some practical way, whether a call, a visit or a ride, the way Deborah went with Barak (v. 9).
4.prayer: Thank God that he hears when his people cry out. Ask for courage to take the next step he has shown you, and for the humility to go alongside others who are afraid.
4.tip: Jael's act will pull the whole discussion toward whether she was right. Say early that Christians read it differently, let people share honestly, and then bring the group back to what the chapter clearly says: God hears the oppressed and gives the victory (vv. 3, 23).

5.open: Tell us about a time you showed up to help with something, like a move, a cleanup or a meal. What made you say yes?
questions: The song begins by praising God because "the people volunteer" (v. 2). Why do you think Deborah thanks God for willing hearts, and not only for the win?
Deborah calls herself "a mother in Israel" (v. 7). Who has played a parent-like role in your faith, and what did they do that mattered?

Verse 8 says, "When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates." Translators are not sure how to read this verse, but it points to a link between turning from God and a life gone wrong. What do people put in God's place today, and what does it cost them?

The song names the tribes that came and the ones that stayed home. Of Reuben it says there was "great indecision" (v. 15). Where are you right now: all in, on the fence, or somewhere you would not say out loud? Answer as honestly as you like.

Verse 20 says "the stars fought" against Sisera, and verse 21 says the river "swept them away." Many readers see a sudden storm and flood here. How do you think about God at work through events that could look like plain weather or luck?
Meroz is cursed because its people "did not come to help the LORD" (v. 23). What do you make of a song that is this hard on people who stayed out of it? How does it sit with you?

Jael is called "most blessed among women" (v. 24), and the song tells of her killing Sisera without apology. Christians read this differently. Some see God's approval, others see an honest record of a violent age. How do you read it, and what questions does it raise for you?

The song ends by picturing Sisera's mother waiting at her window (vv. 28 to 30). How does that picture change the feel of the story? How does it sit beside the closing wish that those who love God "shine like the sun at its brightest" (v. 31)?
5.life: Deborah's song remembers who showed up. This week, thank one person who has quietly shown up for you or for your community, by note, text or in person. Then ask God where he might want you to show up.
5.prayer: Thank God for the people who step forward and serve. Ask for willing hearts in your group, and bring honestly to God any place where you are undecided.
5.tip: Jael and the cursing of Meroz may stir strong reactions. Do not rush to defend or condemn them. Say plainly that Christians read this song differently, let people say how it feels, then bring the group back to what the song says about God, who showed up, and the mother at the window.

6.open: When did you last need a sign or a bit of reassurance before you could make a big decision?
questions: Verses 2 to 6 describe seven years of raids that left Israel "greatly impoverished" (v. 6). What do you picture life was like for ordinary families hiding in caves?
The prophet reminds the people what God had already done for them, then says, "But you did not obey Me" (v. 10). Why do you think remembering the past matters so much when we are in trouble?
The messenger greets Gideon with "O mighty man of valor" while he is hiding wheat in a winepress (vv. 11, 12). Why might God call someone that way when they feel anything but mighty?
Gideon asks, "if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us?" (v. 13). Have you ever asked a question like that? What kind of answer would have felt honest to you?

God tells Gideon, "Go in the strength you have" (v. 14), and Gideon answers that his clan is the weakest and he is the youngest (v. 15). What do you make of God's reply that He will be with him (v. 16)?

Gideon tears down his father's altar to Baal, but does it by night because he was "too afraid" (v. 27). What does it say that God used him even while he was afraid? What is one step of obedience you could take even if you are scared?

Gideon asks for signs with the fleece and says, "Do not be angry with me" (v. 39). Christians differ on whether this shows honest faith or a lack of trust. How do you see it, and how do you bring your doubts to God?
After seeing the angel, Gideon is told, "Peace be with you" (v. 23), and he names the altar The LORD Is Peace (v. 24). Where do you most need that kind of peace right now?
6.life: Think of one thing you have been putting off because you feel too small or too afraid for it. This week, take one small step toward it, and tell God plainly how you feel as you do.
6.prayer: Thank God that He meets frightened and doubting people and says, "I will be with you." Ask Him for honesty about your questions and for courage for one next step.
6.tip: Gideon's question in verse 13 and his fleece tests may stir strong feelings, since some people use fleeces to make decisions and others find them troubling. Say plainly that Christians differ, and notice that God answers Gideon with patience rather than rebuke. Leave room for people who are doubting to speak without being fixed.

7.open: Think of a time you were picked for a team, a job or a task, or left out of one. How did it feel?
questions: God tells Gideon, "You have too many men for Me to deliver Midian into their hands" (v. 2). Why would God make the army smaller before a battle? What do you make of that?

God gives the reason: he did not want Israel to glorify themselves over him and say their own hand had saved them (v. 2). When something goes well in your life, how do you decide how much credit is yours and how much belongs to things beyond your control?
Twenty-two thousand men left because they were "fearful and trembling" (v. 3). What do you think it was like to be one of them, or one of the ten thousand who stayed? What would you have done?

Readers are not sure why God chose the lapping test at the water (vv. 5-7). Some see alert, ready men, and others think the point was just to end up with the smallest group. What do you think, and does it change how you read the story?

God offers Gideon a way to be braver: go down to the camp and listen, "Then your hands will be strengthened" (vv. 10-11). What does it say about God that he gives Gideon this option? What helps you when you are afraid or unsure?
When Gideon hears the soldier's dream, he "bowed in worship" (v. 15). Where have you been surprised by encouragement from an unexpected place, and how did you respond?

The battle is won with trumpets, jars and torches, and the text says "the LORD set all the men in the camp against one another" (v. 22). Where in your life do you feel outnumbered or underqualified? What would it look like to trust God there?

The chapter ends with the heads of Oreb and Zeeb brought to Gideon (v. 25). The story tells this without comment. How do we read the violent parts of the Bible honestly, and what questions does it leave you with?
7.life: Pick one thing this week that you are tempted to handle on your own strength or take credit for. Before you start, tell God it is his, and afterwards tell one person what he did.
7.prayer: Thank God that he works through small, weak and frightened people. Ask for honesty about where you rely on yourself, and for courage to take the next step he gives you.
7.tip: Verses 3 to 7 can leave some people feeling like the ones sent home were failures. Remind the group that the point is about God's strength, not a ranking of who was better. Leave room for quiet people to say they feel more like the men who left than the 300, and let that be an honest answer.

8.open: Think of a time you were part of a group effort and someone felt left out or overlooked. What happened?
questions: The men of Ephraim were angry at being left out, and Gideon answered, "Now what have I accomplished compared to you?" (v. 2). What did his gentle answer do, and when has a humble word calmed an argument for you?
Succoth and Penuel refused to give bread to Gideon's "exhausted" men (vv. 4-8). Why might they have said no, and what do you do when helping someone feels risky?
Gideon promised to punish those towns, and then he did (vv. 16-17). The text tells this bluntly and does not praise it. How do you read that part of the story, and what does it show about Gideon?
In verse 19 Gideon says the men the kings killed at Tabor were his own brothers, sons of his mother. How does grief shape the way he acts here, and how can pain push any of us toward revenge?
When the people offered to make him ruler, Gideon said, "The LORD shall rule over you" (v. 23). What do you admire in that answer, and what does it cost to say something like it?
Gideon made an ephod from the gold, and "it became a snare to Gideon and his household" (v. 27). What good things, even things that begin with good intentions, can quietly become traps for us?
After Gideon died, Israel "failed to remember the LORD their God who had delivered them" (v. 34). What helps you remember what God has done, especially when life is calm and God feels far away?

This chapter is messy. Gideon is faithful in some ways and flawed in others. If you find it hard to see God in a story like this, or hard to trust that he is at work through imperfect people, what makes it hard for you?
8.life: Pick one habit this week that helps you remember what God has done, such as writing down one thing each evening that you are thankful for. Also notice one place where you are tempted to hold on to praise or control, and quietly hand it back to God.
8.prayer: Thank God that he is patient with flawed leaders and flawed people. Ask him to keep you from turning good gifts into idols, and to help you remember his kindness.
8.tip: Verses 16 and 17 are violent, and people may want to defend Gideon or condemn him. Note that Christians differ on whether to read him mainly as a hero of faith or as a warning, and that the text itself reports his revenge without praising it. Then steer the group toward verses 23 to 27, where the chapter's main turn happens.

9.open: Think of a time you picked someone for a team, a job or a committee. What made you choose them?
questions: Abimelech wins Shechem by saying, "Remember that I am your own flesh and blood" (v. 2). Why does an appeal to family loyalty work so well, and what does it cause people to overlook?

The leaders of Shechem gave Abimelech silver from the temple of Baal-berith, and he used it to hire "worthless and reckless men" (v. 4). What does it tell you about this kind of power that it starts with money and hired muscle?

In Jotham's story the olive, the fig and the grapevine each refuse to rule because they would have to stop giving what they were made to give (vv. 9, 11, 13). What do you make of that? When have you seen someone turn down status in order to keep doing something good?
The thornbush is the only one who says yes, and it promises shade it can hardly give (v. 15). Where do you see people today promising more than they can deliver in order to gain power or approval?

Verse 23 says "God sent a spirit of animosity" between Abimelech and Shechem. That is a hard line to read. What questions or discomfort does it raise for you, and what do you notice about the reason given in verse 24?

Abimelech's last concern is how he will be remembered. He does not want people saying a woman killed him (v. 54). What does that say about what drove him his whole life? What are we tempted to protect when we are afraid of looking weak?

Verse 56 says "God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done." Some people find comfort in that and others find it unsettling. Where do you land today, and what would you want to ask God about it?

Jotham speaks the truth and then runs away to live in fear (v. 21). What do you think it was like for him to watch his words come true? Who in your life has spoken a hard truth that no one wanted to hear?
9.life: This week, pay attention to one decision where you are tempted to trust someone mainly because they are familiar, or to back yourself mainly because you want to look strong. Ask instead, what are they actually giving, and what am I?
9.prayer: Ask God to give your group, your church and your leaders humility and honesty. Pray for anyone who has been hurt by people who grabbed power, and ask for courage to tell the truth kindly.
9.tip: This chapter is violent, and verses 23 and 24 can leave people uneasy about how God acts. Do not rush to explain it away. Let people say it is hard, point out that the writer ties the outcome to the murders in verses 56 and 57, and note that Christians differ on whether Jotham's story is against kings in general or only against a bad one.

10.open: When you were a kid, what did you do when you got into trouble and needed someone to bail you out?
questions: Tola and Jair get only a few verses each (vv. 1-5). Why do you think the writer says so little about them? What might a quiet stretch of history teach us?
Verse 6 says Israel served many gods and "did not serve Him." What are some modern things people turn to for security, identity or comfort in place of God?
Verse 7 says "the anger of the LORD burned against Israel." How do you picture God's anger here, and how does it sit with what you know of him as loving?

In verse 10 the people say, "We have sinned against You." Then in verses 11 to 14 God answers with a list of past rescues and tells them to cry out to the gods they chose. What do you hear in that answer?
Israel says in verse 15, "Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!" Have you ever prayed a prayer like that, honest but a bit desperate? What was it like?

Verse 16 says "they put away the foreign gods from among them," and God "could no longer bear the misery of Israel." Readers differ on whether this was real change or mainly a way out of pain. What do you think, and why?
Verse 16 shows God moved by his people's suffering even after they had turned away. What does that tell you about him, and where do you most need to believe it?
If you are in a place where you feel you have wandered, or you are not sure you believe any of this, what would an honest first step toward God look like for you?
10.life: Ask yourself what you tend to run to first when trouble comes. This week, when it happens, pause and say one honest sentence to God before you do anything else.
10.prayer: Thank God that he hears people who cry out, even when they have wandered. Ask him to show each person one thing they are leaning on instead of him, and for the courage to set it down.
10.tip: Verses 13 and 14 can sound harsh, as if God is turning his back. Don't rush to smooth them over. Point the group to verse 16, where God is moved by Israel's misery, and let people say what troubles them. If someone shares a time they felt far from God, receive it kindly without trying to fix it.

11.open: What is a promise you made as a kid that you took completely seriously?
questions: Jephthah's brothers told him, "You shall have no inheritance in our father’s house" (v. 2). What do you think being thrown out by your own family does to a person, and how can that kind of hurt follow someone into adult life?

When the elders come back needing help, Jephthah asks, "Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house?" (v. 7). Why do you think he pushes back before agreeing? How would you respond if people who hurt you came back only when they were in trouble?

Before any fighting, Jephthah sends messengers to argue his case and says, "I have not sinned against you" (v. 27). What do you notice about someone who tries talking first? Where do we skip that step in our own conflicts?

Verse 29 says "the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah," and then in the next verse he makes a vow anyway. Why might someone who already has God's help still feel the need to bargain? Where do you catch yourself bargaining with God?

Jephthah promises that "whatever comes out the door of my house to greet me" will be offered as a burnt offering (v. 31). What do you think he had in mind? Christians read the Hebrew and the ending differently, so what do you make of that?
In verse 35 Jephthah says, "I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back." Is there a point where keeping a promise becomes worse than breaking it? How would you recognize that point?

His daughter says, "Do to me as you have said" (v. 36), and asks only for two months with her friends. What do you notice about her, and why do you think Israel's young women kept remembering her every year (v. 40)?
This chapter is painful and it never says what God thought of the vow. What does it stir up in you, and what would you want to ask God about it? It is fine to say you are unsettled or unsure.
11.life: Before you make a promise this week, even a small one, pause and ask whether you can really keep it and whether it is yours to promise. If you feel stuck in a promise you wish you had never made, talk it over with a trusted friend or pastor.
11.prayer: Thank God that we do not have to bargain to be heard. Pray for people who have been pushed out or rejected, and ask for honesty, wisdom and mercy when we speak too quickly.
11.tip: Verses 34 to 39 are hard, and Christians disagree over whether Jephthah sacrificed his daughter or dedicated her to a life of unmarried service. Name that once, plainly, and do not try to settle it or wrap the story up with a neat lesson. Judges describes what happened without approving it, so let the grief stand, and watch for anyone in the room whose own family story makes this chapter especially heavy.

12.open: Have you ever been teased or sized up for the way you talk, like an accent or a word you say differently?
questions: The men of Ephraim complain, "Why have you crossed over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you?" (v. 1). What do you think was really bothering them? When have you felt left out and reacted with anger?
Jephthah answers that when he called, "you did not save me out of their hands" (v. 2). How does he try to explain himself? What might he have done differently to calm things down?
Verse 4 says the Ephraimites called the Gileadites "fugitives." Why do insults about who belongs cut so deeply, and what did this one lead to?
In verses 5 and 6 a single word, "Shibboleth," decides who lives and who dies. What does it say about this moment in Israel that the people being killed are fellow Israelites?

Verse 6 says "42,000 Ephraimites were killed." Some scholars think the number may describe military units rather than exact thousands, but either way it is a heavy loss. How do you react to reading it? What do you do with a Bible story that is this dark?
Think about a small difference, like an accent, a label or a word, used to decide who is in and who is out. Where do you see that happening today, and what gives such small things so much power?

Ibzan, Elon and Abdon each get only a few lines (vv. 8-15), and the chapter says nothing about what they did. What do you make of leaders who are remembered mostly for their families and where they were buried?
Where in this chapter do you see pride, hurt feelings or fear driving what people do? Where do you see the same things in your own family, church or friendships, and what might help?
12.life: This week, notice one moment when you are tempted to judge someone as an outsider because of how they talk, what they call themselves or where they come from. Pause, and instead ask them a real question about their story.
12.prayer: Ask God to soften pride and wounded feelings in you, and to make you a peacemaker. Pray for a relationship or a group you know that is divided.
12.tip: Verse 7 and Hebrews 11 can raise a hard question: how can someone with such a troubling story be listed among people of faith? Say plainly that Christians disagree about whether to see Jephthah mainly as a hero or as a warning, and don't push for one answer. Keep the focus on what the chapter shows about pride and division. Give a quiet person room to say they find this chapter disturbing.

13.open: Think of a time you were told something wonderful was coming, like a baby, a job or a move. How did you react?
questions: The chapter opens with "Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD" (v. 1). Why do you think this cycle keeps repeating, and where do you see a version of it in everyday life?
The promise comes to a woman who is "barren and had no children" (v. 2). What does it say about God that he comes to her, in a place of long disappointment, before anything else changes?
The angel says her son "will begin the deliverance of Israel" (v. 5). Notice it says begin, not finish. How do you feel about being part of something God starts but you may not see completed?

Manoah prays, "let the man of God You sent us come to us again to teach us how to raise the boy" (v. 8). What does his prayer show about how he saw his job as a parent? How would you describe what it looks like to ask God for help with the people in your care?
The angel won't give his name because it is "beyond comprehension" (v. 18). Is it comforting or frustrating that God is not fully explainable? Be honest about which it is for you right now.

Manoah fears, "We are going to die," but his wife points to what the LORD had actually done: he accepted their offering and spoke to them (vv. 22, 23). When something overwhelming happens, do you lean more toward Manoah's panic or his wife's steady reasoning? What helps you look at the evidence of God's goodness?

Christians read the angel of the LORD differently: some see a created angel speaking for God, others see God himself appearing. What do you take from the scene either way about how close God comes to ordinary people?

The chapter ends quietly: "The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him," and the Spirit "began to stir him" (vv. 24, 25). What do you notice about how God's work often starts small and slowly? Where might that be true in your life, even if you feel unsure or far away?
13.life: Think of one situation that feels stuck or discouraging. This week, write down two or three things God has actually done for you in the past, the way Manoah's wife did, and read them over whenever worry starts to take over.
13.prayer: Thank God for coming near to people who feel overlooked. Ask him for steady trust when things feel overwhelming, and pray for any parents or caregivers in the group.
13.tip: Samson's later story is messy, and people may jump ahead to it. Gently bring the group back to this chapter, which is about God's promise and a couple's response, not about how Samson turns out. Also remember that the question about the angel's identity is one Christians genuinely disagree on, so say so briefly and move on.

14.open: Have you ever made a bet or a dare with friends or family that got out of hand? What happened?
questions: Samson says of the Philistine woman, "she is pleasing to my eyes" (v. 3). His parents want him to marry among his own people. What do you notice about how Samson decides, and how his parents respond?

Verse 4 says his parents "did not know this was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion to move against the Philistines." Readers differ on whether God approved Samson's choice or worked through his stubbornness. What do you make of that?
In verse 6 "the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him" and he killed the lion. Why do you think God gave this strength to someone like Samson? What does that suggest about how God works?

Samson took honey from the lion's carcass and "did not tell them" where it came from (v. 9). Many readers see this as him treating his set apart calling lightly. Where are we tempted to keep quiet about things we know we should not be doing?

The wedding guests tell Samson's wife, "Entice your husband to explain the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father's household to death" (v. 15). What pressures does she face, and what would you have done in her place?
Samson finally told her the answer "because she had pressed him so much" (v. 17). Why do you think he gave in? When has pressure from someone close to you made you say or do something you regretted?

After losing the bet, Samson goes to Ashkelon and kills thirty men to pay what he owes (v. 19). The text says the Spirit came on him but does not praise what he did. How do you weigh a person who does real harm while also being used by God for something larger?

Nobody in this chapter acts very well, yet God is still at work. If you are honestly unsure whether God can use a messy story like yours, or whether he is near at all, what would you say about that tonight?
14.life: Samson hid things and kept secrets, and it cost him. This week, pick one thing you have been keeping hidden or avoiding, and tell God about it plainly. If it feels right, tell one trusted person too.
14.prayer: Thank God that he works even through flawed and stubborn people. Ask him for honesty about our own choices and for patience with those who press us.
14.tip: Verse 19 may stir strong reactions, since it describes killing and the text does not clean it up. Avoid rushing to defend or condemn Samson. Say plainly that Christians read him differently, as a hero God empowered or as a flawed man God used in spite of himself, and keep the group on what the chapter actually shows.

15.open: When you were growing up, how did your family handle it when someone got wronged? Did people forgive quickly, hold a grudge, or get even?
questions: Samson's father-in-law says, "I was sure that you thoroughly hated her," and gives her to another man (v. 2). What went wrong between these two men, and how does a misunderstanding like this grow into something much bigger?

Samson says, "This time I will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines" (v. 3). How does he talk himself into believing he is in the right? When have you caught yourself doing something similar?

The Philistines burn the woman and her father to death (v. 6), and Samson answers with another slaughter (vv. 7-8). Where do you see revenge answering revenge in this chapter, and where do you see it in the world today?

The men of Judah ask, "Do you not realize that the Philistines rule over us?" (v. 11). Why would they hand over one of their own people rather than stand with him? What does that say about living under pressure?

Samson replies, "I have done to them what they did to me" (v. 11). It sounds fair, but how does it keep the cycle going? What might it look like to break a cycle like this in a family, workplace or friendship?
In verse 14 "the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him," even though Samson's motives are far from clean. What does that tell you about how God works through imperfect people?

In verse 18 Samson cries out, "Must I now die of thirst?" It is his first recorded prayer, and it comes when he is empty and worn out. When have you prayed honestly out of need, or struggled to pray at all?
Verse 19 says "God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it." Where have you seen God give help you did not deserve or expect?
15.life: Think of one person you feel you have a score to settle with, big or small. This week, do not answer back in kind. Pray for them by name each day, and notice what changes in you.
15.prayer: Ask God to show us where we are keeping score, and to help us break the cycle of payback. Thank him that he gives help and water in the dry places, even to people who are a mess.
15.tip: Samson's story is violent and he is hard to admire, so people may feel unsure whether to cheer for him or be uncomfortable. Say plainly that Christians read him differently, some as a hero of faith (Hebrews lists him) and some as a flawed man God used in spite of himself, then keep the focus on what the chapter shows about revenge and about God's grace.

16.open: Have you ever kept a secret for a long time and then finally told someone? What made you finally tell?
questions: In verses 1 to 3 Samson tears out the gates of Gaza and carries them away. Why would taking a city's gates have been such a public insult to the Philistines?
Three times Samson gives Delilah a false answer, and each time she tests it (vv. 7-14). What do you notice about how close he lets her get? Why do you think he keeps playing the game?
Verse 16 says she "pressed him daily with her words and pleaded until he was sick to death." Why do you think constant pressure can wear people down, even when they know better?
In verse 17 Samson explains he has been "a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb." What do you think his hair stood for, and why might it matter more than the hair itself?
Verse 20 says "he did not know that the LORD had departed from him." Have you ever drifted from something good without noticing until later? What did that look like?

Samson ends up blind and grinding grain in a prison (v. 21), yet "the hair of his head began to grow back" (v. 22). Where do you see even a small sign of hope in the story? If you are not sure God works that way, what would you want to say about it?
In verse 28 Samson prays, "O Lord GOD, please remember me," and asks for strength to pay back the Philistines. What do you make of God answering a prayer that mixes faith with revenge?
Some Christians see Samson's last act as a hero's sacrifice, and others see it as the tragic end of a self-driven man. Where do you land, and what in the chapter shapes your view?
16.life: Samson trusted the wrong person with what was most precious. This week, think of one person you can be honest with about a struggle or a pressure you are under, and take one step toward telling them. Also tell God where you feel worn down.
16.prayer: Ask God to keep you close when you are tired, pressured or drifting. Thank him that he remembers us, and pray for anyone in the group who feels weak or stuck right now.
16.tip: The chapter opens with Samson and a prostitute and ends with a violent death, and people may get stuck on either. Keep the group on the question of what the story shows about Samson and God, and say plainly that the text tells it without praising or excusing him.

17.open: When you were a kid, what was a rule you or your family made up that nobody else seemed to follow?
questions: Micah admits he took his mother's silver only after he hears she has cursed the thief (vv. 1-2). What do you think finally made him come clean, and what tends to make people own up today?
His mother says, "I wholly dedicate the silver to the LORD," and then uses it to make an idol (v. 3). How can sincere devotion to God still go off track?
Micah builds a shrine, an ephod, household idols and makes his own son a priest (v. 5). What would it look like today to build a faith that is shaped by our own tastes?
Verse 6 says, "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." Where do you see that attitude in the world around you, and where do you catch it in yourself?
The Levite tells Micah he is "on my way to settle wherever I can find a place" (v. 9). How might the need for work, money and security quietly shape what people do with their faith?
Micah says, "Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest" (v. 13). What do we sometimes treat as a guarantee of God's favor?

Christians read the repeated line about having no king in different ways: some see it pointing to Israel's later kings, others see it faulting the people for not treating God as their king. Either way, who or what keeps you honest when you are tempted to make up your own rules?
Be honest here, and pass if you need to: is there a part of your faith that feels more like your own rules than God's, or a part you are simply unsure about? What would help you sort that out?
17.life: This week, pick one habit or belief you hold about God and check it against what Scripture actually says. Pick it by asking, 'Do I believe this because God said it, or because it suits me?' Talk it over with God and one trusted friend.
17.prayer: Thank God that he does not leave us to guess our way through. Ask him to show you where you have been doing what seems right to you, and for the humility to let him lead.
17.tip: This chapter is easy to turn into a lecture about other people's bad religion. Keep it personal and gentle by letting the leader go first in naming a small way they make up their own rules. Remind the group that nobody in the story is beyond God's patience, and that the chapter ends without a verdict, so the next chapter is where the consequences begin.

18.open: Have you ever asked for directions or advice and gotten an answer you were hoping for, only to find out later it was wrong?
questions: The chapter opens with the Danites "looking for territory to occupy" (v. 1). What do you think it feels like to be a group with no settled place to call home? When have you felt that way?

The Danites asked the priest whether their journey would succeed, and he said, "Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey" (v. 6). Why might they have found that answer so easy to believe? Who do you listen to when you want reassurance?
Laish was a place where people were "quiet and unsuspecting" (v. 7). Why does the writer keep pointing this out, and how does it shape the way we read the attack?

The scouts told their brothers, "God has delivered it into your hand" (v. 10). The story never says God told them to go. How can we tell the difference between God leading us and us simply wanting something and putting God's name on it?
When the Danites offered the priest a bigger role, "the priest was glad" and went with them (v. 20). What do you make of his choice? What tempts people to follow whoever offers the better position?

Micah cried, "You took the gods I had made, and my priest... What else do I have?" (v. 24). What does it tell you that his gods could be carried off so easily? What are the things people lean on today that can be taken away just as quickly?

The Danites set up the idol "the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh" (v. 31). Why might a people choose a shrine they control over the place God established? Where do you see that tendency in yourself or in the church today?

Nothing in this chapter is tidy or comforting. If you are honest, what do you feel when you read a story where people do terrible things and no one steps in to stop them? Where do you want to see God in a story like this?
18.life: This week, when you catch yourself wanting advice, pause and ask whether you are seeking the truth or only an answer you hope to hear. Then talk with one trusted person who will tell you honestly what they think.
18.prayer: Ask God for ears that want the truth more than comfort. Pray for people who are vulnerable or overlooked, and for the courage to speak up for them.
18.tip: The attack on Laish is the hardest part, and Christians differ on whether it fits God's earlier promise of the land or is a lawless land grab that the narrator disapproves of. Say that plainly in one line, then steer the group back to what the text shows: the Danites' choices, the priest's easy agreement and the shrine set up away from Shiloh. Let quieter people answer the last question without needing a neat conclusion.

19.open: Think of a time you were on a trip that took much longer than planned. What went wrong, and what do you remember most?
questions: The chapter opens with "no king in Israel" (v. 1). Why do you think the writer starts here, and what does it prepare us to expect?
The woman is never named and never speaks. What do you notice about how each person in the story treats her, from her father to the Levite to the host to the men of the town?
The Levite refuses to stop in a city of "foreigners" and chooses Gibeah because it is an Israelite town (vv. 12, 13). What does the story show us about the safety he expected and the safety he found?
The old man says, "Only do not spend the night in the square" (v. 20). What do you think he knew, and what does his welcome tell us about the difference one person can make?

The host calls the crowd's plan "wicked" (v. 23), then offers his daughter and the concubine instead (v. 24). The Levite then sends her out (v. 25). How do you make sense of good intentions turning into such a terrible choice?
This chapter is hard to read, and it is fine to say so. Where did it leave you today: angry, numb, sad, or unsure what to do with it? Say whatever is honest.

Many older readers saw the Levite as a wronged husband seeking justice, while many modern readers think the writer is exposing his callousness. Christians read him differently. What in the text leads you toward your view?

People say, "Nothing like this has been seen or done" and urge one another to "speak up" (v. 30). What would it look like for a community to truly see someone hurt like this and act, rather than only being shocked?
19.life: Pay attention this week to one person who is easy to overlook or who rarely gets heard, at work, church or in your street. Do one small, real thing to listen to them or stand with them.
19.prayer: Ask God to be near everyone who has been hurt and not been listened to. Ask for eyes to see people who are overlooked and the courage to act on their behalf.
19.tip: This chapter describes sexual violence, and someone in the room may have personal pain connected to it. Name that at the start, do not push anyone to speak, and do not rush to find a lesson or defend the passage. It is fine to simply grieve what was done to her, and say plainly that none of it was her fault. Offer to talk privately afterward with anyone who needs it, and know who you would point them to for further help.

20.open: Think of a time a disagreement with family or friends got bigger than anyone meant it to. What helped, or what didn't?
questions: The tribes come together "as one man" to deal with a terrible crime (v. 1). What does the text show us about why they gathered and what they wanted?

The Levite tells the story of what happened at Gibeah (vv. 4-7). Many readers notice that he leaves out his own part in it from chapter 19. Why might people tell a story in a way that makes themselves look better?

The tribes first ask Benjamin to "hand over the wicked men of Gibeah" (v. 13), but Benjamin refuses. What do you think made Benjamin dig in, and when have you seen a group protect its own people when it should not have?

Israel loses 22,000 men and then 18,000 more (vv. 21, 25), even after asking God what to do. The text never says why. What do you make of that, and how do you handle it when you do something that seems right and it still goes badly?
After the second loss the people "sat weeping before the LORD" and fasted (v. 26). What stands out to you about how they responded in grief and confusion?

By the end, Israel's army burns the towns of Benjamin and kills people and animals, leaving the tribe almost gone (v. 48). Where does justice seem to turn into something else in this chapter, and how could anyone tell?
Israel keeps calling Benjamin "our brothers" (v. 23), yet the chapter ends with brothers destroying each other. What does that say about how conflict can grow inside a family, a church or a nation?
This is a hard chapter, and God's part in it can be unsettling to read. If you are unsure what to make of it, or of God in it, what questions would you honestly like to bring to him?
20.life: Think of one conflict or grudge you are part of right now. Before you act or speak this week, pause and ask God whether you want to see wrong put right or simply want to win. Then take one small step toward honesty or peace.
20.prayer: Ask God for wisdom to seek justice without cruelty and to stay humble when we are sure we are right. Pray for anyone in the group caught in a painful conflict, and for people who have been hurt by violence.
20.tip: This chapter is violent and the earlier crime is disturbing, so go gently, since someone in the room may carry their own story of abuse. Christians read it differently: some see God-backed justice that Israel then carried too far, others see a nation coming apart. Name that in one line, don't push for a single verdict, and let people say honestly that it troubles them.

21.open: Can you think of a time you tried to fix a mistake and ended up making things more complicated?
questions: The people wept and cried out to God, asking why one tribe was missing from Israel (v. 3). Their own war had caused the loss. What does it say about us when we ask God why, but skip asking what we did?
Israel had sworn "Not one of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjamite" (v. 1). Why do you think they treated an oath as more binding than the people it was hurting?

In verses 10 and 11 the army is sent to Jabesh-gilead to put the people to the sword, and only 400 young women are spared. What stands out to you about how this decision is described, and about what is left unsaid?
Verse 15 says the people grieved "because the LORD had made a void in the tribes of Israel." How do you hear that line, given that Israel's own choices led there?
The elders find a loophole: since the fathers "did not actually give them your daughters," there is "no guilt" (v. 22). Where do we use technicalities to feel clean about something we know is wrong?
The women of Jabesh-gilead and the dancers at Shiloh are taken, and the text never says what they wanted or felt. Why might the writer leave their voices out, and how should we read that silence?
The book ends with "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (v. 25). Where do you see that mindset today, and where do you see it in your own life?
If you find this chapter hard to read, or hard to square with your picture of God, what part troubles you most? There is room in this group to say so honestly.
21.life: This week, notice one place where you are trying to fix a problem in a way that quietly hurts someone else, or where you are leaning on a technicality. Name it to God, and if you can, to someone you trust.
21.prayer: Ask God for honesty about the harm we cause while trying to do good. Pray for people who are voiceless or taken advantage of, and ask for the humility to let God be the one we answer to.
21.tip: This chapter describes violence against women and the narrator does not approve or condemn it outright, so some people will be upset and others will want to explain it away. Say plainly that the text records these acts without endorsing them, that Christians read the silence differently, and that it is fine to be troubled. Keep the group focused on the final verse and what the story shows about life when people do what seems right to them.
